title: Searching for MobileNetV3
authors: Andrew Howard, Mark Sandler, Grace Chu, Liang-Chieh Chen, Bo Chen, Mingxing Tan, Weijun Wang, Yukun Zhu, Ruoming Pang, Vijay Vasudevan, Quoc V. Le, Hartwig Adam

pages.title: The core idea
pages.subtitle: Co-design the architecture by search, then hand-tune

blocks.html: The problem. You want a neural network that recognizes objects on a phone — fast enough to run in real time, small enough to fit, accurate enough to be useful. Every millisecond and every megabyte counts. MobileNetV3 is a family of such models, and its central idea is to combine automated architecture search with targeted hand engineering: let an algorithm search for a good backbone, then have humans fix the few parts the search misses.

Analogy. Think of designing a fuel-efficient car. An optimization program can search thousands of engine and chassis configurations to find one that is fast and economical — but it might miss that the rear spoiler (a single bolted-on part) is creating most of the drag. A human engineer spots that instantly and redesigns it by hand. MobileNetV3 uses exactly this division of labor: search for the bulk of the design, hand-fix the few glaringly expensive parts.

Two search techniques work together. Platform-aware NAS (neural architecture search) finds the coarse structure of each block, optimizing for accuracy under a latency budget on real hardware. Then NetAdapt tunes the number of filters in each layer, one at a time. Finally the authors redesign the most expensive layers by hand and introduce a new, cheaper activation function.

We achieve new state of the art results for mobile classification, detection and segmentation ... MobileNetV3-Large is 3.2% more accurate on ImageNet classification while reducing latency by 20% compared to MobileNetV2.

The payoff. Two models for two budgets: MobileNetV3-Large (about 75.2% top-1 ImageNet accuracy, ~20% lower latency than MobileNetV2) for higher-resource phones, and MobileNetV3-Small (about 67.4% top-1) for very tight budgets. Both push the accuracy-vs-latency frontier outward — for any given speed, they are more accurate than what came before.

Context. This is the third generation of Google’s MobileNet line (V1 in 2017, V2 in 2018), and a landmark in the move from hand-designed to searched efficient networks. It folds in ideas from across 2018–2019 efficient-net research — MnasNet’s latency-aware search, Squeeze-and-Excitation attention, and the swish activation — and packages them into a practical, deployable recipe.

The problem. The obvious way to measure a model’s cost is to count its multiply-add operations (FLOPs). But on a real phone, what users feel is wall-clock latency, and that depends on far more than arithmetic: memory bandwidth, cache behavior, how cleanly an operation maps to the chip’s instruction set, and fixed overheads per layer.

Concrete example. A depthwise convolution and a regular convolution can have wildly different FLOP-to-latency ratios. A layer might be cheap in multiply-adds yet memory-bound and therefore slow; another might look expensive on paper but run fast because it keeps the hardware’s arithmetic units busy. The sigmoid inside the swish activation is a perfect case: tiny FLOP count, but it needs an exponential, which mobile CPUs compute slowly and quantize poorly. Optimizing FLOPs would never catch this.

The approach. MobileNetV3 therefore optimizes directly against measured latency on the target device, and treats network design as a search problem rather than a purely manual one. Humans are good at spotting a few structural inefficiencies; search is good at exploring thousands of configurations. The paper uses both, each where it is strongest.

The inherited foundation. MobileNetV3 does not start from scratch. From MobileNetV1 it inherits the depthwise-separable convolution: instead of one fat convolution that filters spatially and mixes channels at once, you split it into (1) a depthwise convolution that applies one spatial filter per channel independently, and (2) a $1\times1$ pointwise convolution that mixes channels. For a $3\times3$ filter this cuts cost by roughly $8\!-\!9\times$ with little accuracy loss.

From MobileNetV2 it inherits the inverted residual with linear bottleneck: the block expands a thin input to a wide intermediate representation (where the cheap depthwise filtering happens), then projects back down to a thin output with no activation on that final projection (the ‘linear bottleneck’, which preserves information that ReLU would destroy in low dimensions), with a residual skip connection between the thin ends. MobileNetV3 layers its new ideas — SE attention, h-swish, searched sizing — on top of this block.

The problem. The space of possible networks is astronomically large — how many blocks, how wide each one, what kernel sizes, where to put attention. You cannot try them all. MobileNetV3 splits the search into two stages working at two granularities: one finds the coarse skeleton, the other trims it precisely.

Stage 1 — Platform-aware NAS (the skeleton). Reusing the MnasNet approach, a controller searches the global block structure — how many blocks, their kernel sizes, expansion ratios — to maximize a reward that explicitly trades off accuracy against real on-device latency. The reward has the form $\text{ACC}(m) \times [\text{LAT}(m)/\text{TAR}]^{w}$, balancing model accuracy $\text{ACC}(m)$ against its latency $\text{LAT}(m)$ relative to a target $\text{TAR}$. This produces a strong starting architecture tuned to the hardware.

Stage 2 — NetAdapt (the fine trim). Starting from the NAS skeleton, NetAdapt refines it layer by layer. Each round it proposes a set of small changes — each shrinking the filter count of one layer — briefly fine-tunes each candidate, measures the real latency and accuracy of each, and keeps the proposal with the best accuracy-per-latency trade-off. It repeats until the latency target is met. The selection criterion maximizes:

Reading it: $\Delta\text{Acc}$ is how much accuracy a proposed filter reduction loses (a small negative number) and $\Delta\text{latency}$ is how much latency it saves. The ratio rewards proposals that shed the most latency for the least accuracy cost — cut the fat, keep the muscle.

items: Platform-aware NAS: searches coarse, block-level structure under a latency-aware reward — sets the skeleton.
NetAdapt: greedily fine-tunes per-layer filter counts using measured on-device latency — trims the fat.
Complementary scopes: NAS handles global structure (slow, broad); NetAdapt handles local sizing (fast, precise).

blocks.html: Why two stages. NAS alone is expensive and tends to find good structure but coarse sizing; NetAdapt is cheap and precise but cannot invent new structure. Chaining them gets the best of both. Trivia: this latency-aware, two-stage recipe became the template for nearly all later mobile architecture search.

The problem. Search optimizes the average block, but it tends to leave a couple of layers that are accurate yet disproportionately slow — the early stem and the final classifier head. These sit at the network’s edges, where feature maps are either very large (the stem, on the full-resolution image) or where channel counts balloon (the head). The authors fix these by hand.

Fix 1 — the efficient last stage. The original MobileNetV2 head expanded to a wide $1\times1$ layer (e.g. 960→1280 channels) before the final spatial pooling, so that expensive expansion ran over the whole feature map. MobileNetV3 moves the expensive $1\times1$ expansion to after the average pooling, where the spatial size is just $1\times1$ — the same representational power, but the costly operation now runs on a single pixel instead of a $7\times7$ grid. This drops about 7 milliseconds (~11% of runtime) with no measurable accuracy loss.

Fix 2 — a leaner stem. The initial convolution had 32 filters; the authors found 16 filters with h-swish maintain the same accuracy, saving another ~2 ms. Small layer, but it runs on the largest feature map, so it punches above its weight.

Fix 3 — Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention. Inside the bottleneck blocks, MobileNetV3 adds lightweight SE modules. An SE module is a cheap form of channel attention: it (1) squeezes each channel’s spatial map to a single number via global average pooling, (2) passes those through a tiny two-layer bottleneck network to learn a per-channel importance weight in $[0,1]$, then (3) rescales each channel by its weight. This lets the network emphasize informative channels and suppress useless ones, boosting accuracy for negligible cost. (V3 uses the hard-sigmoid for the SE gate, and reduces the SE bottleneck to 1/4 of the expansion channels to keep it cheap.)

Why search misses these. SE placement and the head redesign are structural choices outside the search space the authors gave NAS; and the stem/head sit at extreme feature-map sizes where a human’s understanding of where compute is spent beats brute-force search. This is the ‘search plus craft’ thesis in action.

The problem. The swish activation, $\text{swish}(x) = x \cdot \sigma(x)$ (where $\sigma$ is the sigmoid), was found to improve accuracy over ReLU in deep networks. But the sigmoid $\sigma(x) = 1/(1+e^{-x})$ requires an exponential, which is slow on mobile CPUs and behaves badly under fixed-point quantization (the conversion to cheap 8-bit integer math used on-device). On a phone, swish’s accuracy gain is eaten by its compute cost.
The idea. Replace the expensive sigmoid with a piecewise-linear look-alike that hardware already runs fast. MobileNetV3 defines hard-swish (h-swish):

Reading it term by term: $\text{ReLU6}(z) = \min(\max(z, 0), 6)$ is a ReLU clipped at 6 — an operation mobile chips already implement as a single fast instruction. The factor $\frac{\text{ReLU6}(x+3)}{6}$ is a cheap piecewise-linear approximation of $\sigma(x)$: it is 0 for $x \le -3$, rises linearly to 1 by $x \ge 3$, and so multiplies $x$ much like swish does — but with only additions, a clamp, and a multiply. No exponential, and it quantizes cleanly because it is exactly piecewise-linear.
The same trick for the SE gate. The SE module’s sigmoid gate is likewise replaced by a hard-sigmoid, $\text{ReLU6}(x+3)/6$, for the same speed and quantization reasons.

Why apply it selectively. The authors use h-swish only in the deeper half of the network. Activation cost scales with feature-map size, and the early layers have the largest maps; the deeper layers (smaller maps, more channels) are where the nonlinearity helps accuracy most while costing least. This selective placement captures most of swish’s benefit at a fraction of the cost.

Trivia. The ‘hard’ prefix — hard-swish, hard-sigmoid — comes from earlier ‘hard’ piecewise-linear versions of saturating functions used in quantized and recurrent nets. MobileNetV3 popularized them for efficient vision, and h-swish remains a standard building block in mobile model libraries today.

The headline. On ImageNet (1.28M training images, 1000 classes; top-1 = fraction where the single top guess is correct), MobileNetV3-Large reaches about 75.2% top-1 while being roughly 20% faster than MobileNetV2 (measured on a Pixel phone). MobileNetV3-Small targets the very-low-latency regime at about 67.4% top-1, beating prior small models at similar speed.
The ablations — every ingredient earns its place. The paper peels back each addition from MobileNetV3-Large to show its individual contribution to accuracy and latency:

Reading the ablation. Search lifts accuracy ~2 points and trims latency; SE adds accuracy but a touch of latency; h-swish adds accuracy and claws latency back; the efficient last stage is pure latency savings (~7 ms) at constant accuracy. None of these alone is dramatic — the win is the cumulative stack.

Why it matters. The result is not just ‘a faster model’ but a demonstration that the speed-accuracy frontier can be pushed outward by method — latency-aware search plus targeted craft — rather than by simply scaling up. For any latency budget you care about, V3 gives more accuracy than its predecessors.

pages.title: Detection and segmentation
pages.subtitle: The backbone transfers; LR-ASPP for pixels

blocks.html: The question. A good classification backbone should transfer to harder tasks. Does MobileNetV3 help when you need where objects are, not just what they are?

Detection. Plugged into an SSDLite detector as the feature extractor, MobileNetV3-Large improves the speed-accuracy trade-off on COCO over MobileNetV2 — comparable mAP (mean average precision) at lower latency. The same SE/h-swish/searched backbone that helped classification helps detection, confirming the features are generally useful.

Segmentation — LR-ASPP. For semantic segmentation (labeling every pixel with a class), the paper introduces Lite Reduced ASPP (LR-ASPP), a stripped-down efficient version of the Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling head used in DeepLab. It combines a large-kernel global-context branch (via pooling) with a $1\times1$ branch and lightweight bilinear upsampling, replacing the heavy multi-rate atrous convolutions of the original. Paired with the V3 backbone, it delivers strong Cityscapes accuracy at low latency.
MobileNetV3-Large LR-ASPP is 34% faster than MobileNetV2 R-ASPP at similar accuracy for Cityscapes segmentation.

Why this matters. Showing the backbone wins across classification, detection, and segmentation establishes MobileNetV3 as a general-purpose efficient feature extractor — the role it went on to play across countless on-device vision products.

MobileNetV3 showed that the best efficient models come from combining automated search with human insight, and from optimizing against measured hardware latency rather than proxy FLOPs. Its individual components — h-swish, SE inside mobile blocks, the efficient last stage — became standard ingredients in later efficient architectures.

items: Combined platform-aware NAS (global structure) with NetAdapt (per-layer filter sizing) under a real-latency objective.
Hand-redesigned the expensive stem and last stage and added squeeze-and-excitation channel attention to the bottleneck blocks.
Introduced h-swish and hard-sigmoid — quantization-friendly, exponential-free activations.
MobileNetV3-Large: ~75.2% ImageNet top-1, ~20% faster than V2; Small: ~67.4%; strong detection (SSDLite) and segmentation (LR-ASPP) transfer.

blocks.html: The bigger picture. Coming out of the same Google research effort as MnasNet and EfficientNet, MobileNetV3 cemented latency-aware NAS as the default way to design mobile networks and remains a widely-deployed, widely-cited backbone. Its ‘let search do the bulk, let humans fix the edges’ philosophy is now conventional wisdom in efficient deep learning.
